blocks.html: A computer is an electronic device that accepts data as input, processes it according to a set of instructions (a program), stores it, and produces useful output.
Think of a computer like a kitchen in a restaurant:

items.html: The order slip is the input (data).
The chef is the processor, who follows the recipe (the program).
The fridge and shelves are memory and storage.
The cooked dish served to you is the output (information).

blocks.html: Every computer works on the IPO cycle: Input → Process → Output, with Storage supporting each step.

rows: Performs billions of operations per second
A modern CPU runs at 3–5 GHz
Gives correct results if data and program are correct (GIGO: Garbage In, Garbage Out)
Stores huge amounts of data permanently
A 1 TB hard disk holds about 2.5 lakh photos
Can do many different kinds of tasks
Cannot think on its own; follows instructions only
It cannot decide what you want without a program

blocks.html: A computer system has two parts: hardware (the physical parts you can touch) and software (the programs that tell hardware what to do). The hardware is organised into four units: input unit, central processing unit (CPU), memory unit and output unit.
The input unit takes data from the user and converts it into binary (0s and 1s) that the computer understands.
Examples: keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone, webcam, touch screen, barcode reader, biometric scanner (used in Aadhaar), joystick.
The CPU is the "brain" of the computer. It has three parts:

items.html: Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU): Performs arithmetic operations (+, −, ×, ÷) and logical operations (comparisons such as >, <, ==, AND, OR).
Control Unit (CU): Directs all operations. It fetches instructions from memory, decodes them and tells other units what to do, like a traffic police officer.
Registers: Very small, very fast storage locations inside the CPU that hold the data and instruction being used right now.

blocks.html: Stores data and instructions before, during and after processing. (Explained in detail in Section 1.4.)
The output unit converts the binary result into a form humans can understand.
Examples: monitor, printer, speaker, projector, plotter, headphones.
Machine cycle: The CPU repeats four steps for every instruction: Fetch → Decode → Execute → Store.

blocks.caption: Figure 1.1 · Block diagram of a computer

blocks.html: The CPU sits at the centre: it takes data from the input unit, works with the memory unit in both directions, and sends results to the output unit.

blocks.html: Moore's Law: Gordon Moore observed in 1965 that the number of transistors on a chip doubles roughly every two years.
Memory stores data and instructions. It is measured in bits and bytes.
Memory hierarchy (fastest and costliest at top): Registers → Cache → Primary memory (RAM) → Secondary storage (SSD/HDD).
Going down the pyramid, each level holds more data at a lower cost per byte, but the CPU reaches it more slowly.
(a) Registers — inside the CPU; fastest; smallest.
(b) Cache Memory — a small, fast memory between the CPU and RAM. It keeps the data the CPU uses most often, so the CPU does not wait for slower RAM. Levels: L1, L2, L3.
(c) Primary Memory — directly accessed by the CPU.

rows: Volatile: data is lost when power goes off
Types: SRAM (faster, used in cache), DRAM (used as main memory)
Example: 8 GB RAM in a laptop
Example: BIOS chip on the motherboard

blocks.html: (d) Secondary Memory — permanent, large and cheaper storage, not directly accessed by the CPU.
Examples: Hard Disk Drive (HDD), Solid State Drive (SSD), pen drive, memory card, CD/DVD/Blu-ray, magnetic tape, cloud storage.

lessons.title: 1.5 Data Transfer Between Memory and CPU

blocks.html: Data moves between the CPU, memory and devices through a set of wires called a bus. There are three types:

items.html: Data bus: Carries the actual data. It is bidirectional (both ways).
Address bus: Carries the memory address where data is to be read or written. It is unidirectional (CPU → memory).
Control bus: Carries control signals such as read, write and interrupt.

blocks.html: All three together are called the system bus. Think of it like a courier service: the address bus is the delivery address, the data bus is the parcel, and the control bus is the instruction "deliver" or "pick up".
A microprocessor is a CPU built on a single integrated-circuit chip. Examples: Intel Core i5/i7, AMD Ryzen, Apple M-series, Qualcomm Snapdragon (phones).

items.html: Word size: Number of bits the CPU processes at once (32-bit or 64-bit).
Memory size: How much RAM it can address. A 32-bit CPU can address at most 4 GB.
Clock speed: Number of cycles per second, measured in GHz (1 GHz = 10⁹ cycles per second).
Cores: Independent processing units on one chip (dual-core, quad-core, octa-core).
Instruction set: CISC (Complex Instruction Set, e.g. Intel x86) or RISC (Reduced Instruction Set, e.g. ARM in phones).

blocks.html: Microcontroller: A small computer on one chip that has a CPU, memory and input/output ports together. Used in washing machines, microwave ovens, remote controls, Arduino boards and car systems.

rows: Only the CPU on a chip
CPU + RAM + ROM + I/O on one chip

items.html: Data is raw facts and figures with no meaning on their own. Example: 85, 92, 78.
Information is processed data that has meaning. Example: "Riya's average marks are 85."

blocks.html: Software is a set of programs and instructions that tells the hardware what to do. Without software, hardware is like a body without a brain.
(a) System Software — manages and controls the hardware.

items.html: Operating system: Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, iOS
System utilities: antivirus, disk cleanup, disk defragmenter, file compression (WinZip), backup tools
Device drivers: small programs that let the OS talk to a specific device, such as a printer driver

blocks.html: (b) Programming Tools (Language Translators) — convert programs written by humans into machine code.

items.html: Assembler: Converts assembly language into machine code.
Compiler: Converts the whole program into machine code at once, then runs it. C and C++ use a compiler (for example, g++ ).
Interpreter: Converts and runs the program one line at a time. Python and JavaScript use an interpreter.

rows: Translates the whole program at once
Translates one line at a time
Shows all errors together after compiling

blocks.html: (c) Application Software — helps users do specific tasks.

items.html: General purpose: MS Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Google Chrome, VLC Player, Photoshop
Customised (tailor-made): School management software, hospital billing software, IRCTC railway booking system

blocks.html: Free and Open Source Software (FOSS): Software whose source code is free to use, study and change. Examples: Linux, LibreOffice, Firefox, GIMP, Code::Blocks.
Proprietary software: Owned by a company; source code is secret and a licence is needed. Examples: MS Windows, MS Office, Adobe Photoshop.
An operating system (OS) is system software that acts as an interface between the user and the hardware, and manages all the resources of the computer.

items.html: Command-line interface (CLI): The user types commands. Example: MS-DOS, Linux terminal.
Graphical user interface (GUI): The user clicks icons and menus. Example: Windows, macOS.
Touch-based interface: Example: Android, iOS.
Voice-based interface: Example: Google Assistant, Siri, Alexa.
Gesture-based interface: Example: smart TVs, VR headsets.
Process management: Decides which program uses the CPU and for how long (multitasking).
Memory management: Allocates RAM to programs and frees it when they close.
File management: Creates, stores, names, copies and deletes files and folders.
Device management: Controls input/output devices through device drivers.
Security: Protects data with passwords, user accounts and permissions.

Example 2: Bits in a file. A text file is 2 KB. How many bits does it contain?

Example 3: Photos on a pen drive. A 16 GB pen drive is to store photos of 4 MB each. How many photos fit?
Number of photos = 16,384 ÷ 4 = 4096 photos
Example 4: Addressable memory. A computer has a 16-bit address bus. How much memory can it address?
Number of addresses = 2¹⁶ = 65,536
If each address holds 1 byte, memory = 65,536 bytes = 65,536 ÷ 1024 = 64 KB
(Similarly, a 32-bit address bus can address 2³² bytes = 4 GB.)
Example 5: Download time. A 700 MB movie is downloaded at 5 MB per second. How long will it take?
Time = 700 ÷ 5 = 140 seconds = 2 minutes 20 seconds

blocks.html: 1. Define a computer. Write any two of its characteristics.

Answer: A computer is an electronic device that takes data as input, processes it using a program and gives meaningful output. Two characteristics: (i) Speed — it performs billions of operations per second; (ii) Accuracy — it gives correct results when the input and program are correct.
2. What is the difference between data and information? Give one example.
Answer: Data is raw, unprocessed facts with no meaning by itself; information is processed data that has meaning. Example: the marks 72, 85, 90 are data; "The class average is 82.3" is information.
3. Name the three components of the CPU.
Answer: (i) Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU), (ii) Control Unit (CU), (iii) Registers.
4. Why is cache memory used?

Answer: Cache memory is a small, very fast memory placed between the CPU and RAM. It stores frequently used data and instructions, so the CPU gets them quickly instead of waiting for the slower RAM. This increases the overall speed of the computer.
5. Differentiate between RAM and ROM (any two points).

rows: Volatile: data is lost when power is off

blocks.html: 6. What is a bus? Name its types.
Answer: A bus is a set of wires that carries data, addresses and control signals between the CPU, memory and other devices. Types: (i) Data bus, (ii) Address bus, (iii) Control bus.
7. Convert 5 MB into bytes.
Answer: 5 MB = 5 × 1024 KB = 5120 KB = 5120 × 1024 bytes = 5,242,880 bytes.
8. What is a device driver? Give an example.
Answer: A device driver is system software that allows the operating system to communicate with a particular hardware device. Example: a printer driver lets Windows send documents to the printer.
9. Differentiate between a compiler and an interpreter (any two points).

rows: Translates the whole program at once
Translates one line at a time
Creates an executable file; example: C++ (g++ )

blocks.html: 10. What is a microcontroller? Name two devices that use it.
Answer: A microcontroller is a small computer on a single chip with a processor, memory and input/output ports. Devices: washing machine and microwave oven.
11. What is meant by "word size" of a microprocessor?

Answer: Word size is the number of bits a processor can process in one operation. A 64- bit processor handles 64 bits at once, so it processes data faster and can address more memory than a 32-bit processor.
12. What is Free and Open Source Software? Give two examples.
Answer: FOSS is software whose source code is freely available to use, study, modify and share. Examples: Linux and LibreOffice.
13. Name any four input devices and two output devices.
Answer: Input: keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone. Output: monitor, printer.
14. What is the stored-program concept?

Answer: Given by John von Neumann, it means that both the program (instructions) and the data are stored together in the computer's memory. The CPU fetches instructions one by one from memory and executes them.
15. Why is the header file <iostream> used in a C++ program?
Answer: <iostream> (input-output stream) contains the definitions of cin and cout . Without including it, a C++ program cannot take input from the keyboard or display output on the screen.
16. Why is a computer said to have "no IQ"?
Answer: A computer cannot think or take decisions on its own. It only follows the instructions given in a program. If the program or data is wrong, the output will also be wrong (GIGO).
1. Draw a block diagram of a computer and explain each unit.

items.html: Input unit: Accepts data and instructions from the user and converts them into binary. Examples: keyboard, mouse, scanner.
CPU: Processes the data.
ALU performs arithmetic (+, −, ×, ÷) and logical (>, <, ==) operations.
CU fetches, decodes and controls the execution of instructions, and coordinates all units.
Registers hold the data and instructions currently being processed.
Memory unit: Stores data and programs before, during and after processing. Primary memory (RAM, ROM) is used by the CPU directly; secondary memory (HDD, SSD) stores data permanently.
Output unit: Converts the binary result into human-readable form. Examples: monitor, printer, speaker.

blocks.html: 2. Explain the memory hierarchy with a diagram. Why is it needed?

blocks.code:
/\
           /  \        Registers    (fastest, smallest, costliest)
          /----\
         / Cache\      L1, L2, L3
        /--------\
       /   RAM    \    Primary memory
      /------------\
     /  SSD / HDD   \  Secondary storage
    /----------------\
   / Cloud / Tape /DVD\ (slowest, largest, cheapest)
  /--------------------\

blocks.html: As we move down the pyramid, speed decreases, cost per byte decreases and storage capacity increases.

Why it is needed: Fast memory is very costly, so a computer cannot have a large amount of it. Slow memory is cheap and large. The hierarchy gives a balance: the CPU keeps the data it needs right now in fast registers and cache, the running programs in RAM, and everything else in cheap secondary storage. This gives good speed at a reasonable cost.

blocks.html: 4. What is an operating system? Explain any four functions of an OS.
Answer: An operating system is system software that acts as an interface between the user and the computer hardware, and manages all the computer's resources. Examples: Windows, Linux, Android.

items.html: Process management: Creates, schedules and ends processes. It shares CPU time among programs so many can run together (multitasking).
Memory management: Allocates RAM to each program when it starts and frees it when it ends, and keeps one program from using another's memory.
File management: Organises data into files and folders, and handles creating, naming, copying, moving and deleting them.
Device management: Controls input/output devices using device drivers and manages their queues (for example, a print queue).
Security: Protects data with passwords, user accounts and access permissions.

items.html: Editing: The programmer writes source code in an editor and saves it as

items.html: Preprocessing: The preprocessor handles lines starting with # , such as #include <iostream> , by inserting the header file's content.

blocks.html: 1. (a) Describe the evolution of computers from the abacus to modern AI systems. (5)

blocks.text: (b) Explain the five generations of computers with their technology, features and examples. (5) Answer (a):

items.html: Abacus (about 500 BC): A frame of beads for counting; the earliest calculating tool.
Pascaline (1642): Blaise Pascal's mechanical machine that could add and subtract.
Analytical Engine (1834): Charles Babbage designed it with input, a "mill" (processor), a "store" (memory) and output — the plan of a modern computer. Ada Lovelace wrote the first algorithm for it.
Tabulating Machine (1890): Herman Hollerith used punched cards to process the US census; his company later became IBM.
Turing Machine (1937) and Von Neumann architecture (1945): Turing gave the theory of computation; von Neumann gave the stored-program concept used in every computer today.
ENIAC (1946): The first general-purpose electronic computer, built with about 18,000 vacuum tubes.
Transistor (1947), IC (1958), Microprocessor (1971): Each made computers smaller, faster and cheaper. Intel 4004 was the first microprocessor.
Personal computers (1981), internet (1990s), smartphones (2007), AI and cloud (2010s onwards): Computing moved from labs to homes, pockets and the internet.

rows: Very large, produced a lot of heat, used machine language, punched cards for input
Smaller, faster, less heat, assembly language and early high-level languages (FORTRAN, COBOL)
Keyboard and monitor used, operating systems, multiprogramming
Personal computers, GUI, networking, internet, C and C++ languages
IBM PC, Apple Macintosh, modern laptops
AI, ULSI, parallel and quantum processing
Natural language understanding, machine learning, robotics, voice assistants
AI assistants, self- driving cars, IBM Watson

blocks.html: 2. (a) What is memory? Explain primary, secondary and cache memory with examples. (6) (b) A school stores 1200 student photos of 2.5 MB each and 1200 report cards of 200 KB each. Find the total storage needed in GB. (4)
Answer (a): Memory is the part of a computer that stores data and instructions. It is measured in bits and bytes.

items.html: Primary memory is directly accessed by the CPU and holds programs currently running.
RAM: Volatile, read-write. Types: SRAM (fast, used for cache) and DRAM (main memory). Example: 8 GB DDR4 RAM.
ROM: Non-volatile, read-only. Stores BIOS/firmware. Types: PROM (written once), EPROM (erased by UV light), EEPROM (erased electrically).

Cache memory is a very fast, small memory between the CPU and RAM. It holds frequently used data so the CPU does not wait for RAM. It has levels L1 (inside the core, fastest), L2 and L3 (shared by cores).
Secondary memory is permanent, large and cheap, and is not directly accessed by the CPU. Data is first loaded into RAM.
Magnetic: hard disk, magnetic tape
Optical: CD, DVD, Blu-ray
Solid state: SSD, pen drive, memory card
Cloud storage: Google Drive, OneDrive

blocks.html: Photos = 1200 × 2.5 MB = 3000 MB
In GB = 3234.375 ÷ 1024 = about 3.16 GB

Answer (a): Software is a set of programs that tells the hardware what to do.

items.html: System software: Controls hardware and runs the computer. Includes the operating system (Windows, Linux), utilities (antivirus, disk defragmenter, backup) and device drivers (printer, graphics).
Programming tools: Help create programs. Includes language translators (assembler, compiler, interpreter) and IDEs (Code::Blocks, VS Code).

Why C++: C++ is compiled, so programs run fast. It teaches students how memory, data types and the CPU really work. It is widely used in system software, games, competitive programming and engineering entrance exams, and it forms a strong base for learning Java, C# and Python later.

blocks.html: 4. (a) Explain how data is transferred between the CPU and memory using the system bus. Draw a diagram. (5) (b) Explain the functions of an operating system and the different types of user interfaces. (5)
Answer (a): The CPU and memory are connected by the system bus, made of three buses:

items.html: Address bus: The CPU puts the address of the memory location it wants. Unidirectional. Its width decides how much memory can be used (2ⁿ locations for an n-bit bus).
Data bus: Carries the actual data between CPU and memory. Bidirectional. Its width (32/64 bits) decides how much data moves at once.
Control bus: Carries signals like READ, WRITE, clock and interrupt that control the transfer.

blocks.html: Reading data: The CPU puts the address on the address bus → sends a READ signal on the control bus → memory places the data on the data bus → the CPU receives it.
Writing data: The CPU puts the address on the address bus and the data on the data bus → sends a WRITE signal → memory stores the data at that address.
Answer (b): Functions: process management, memory management, file management, device management and security (explained in 5-mark Q4).
